track.name: psychology
track.label: Behavioral Psychology
track.summary: Learn how people actually decide and behave — heuristics, biases, motivation, and habit formation — so you can design products, marketing, and policies that work with human nature instead of against it.

phases.title: Foundations of Judgment & Decision-Making
phases.description: How the mind actually makes decisions — the two systems of thinking and the mental shortcuts behind everyday judgment.

phases.title: Cognitive Biases in Practice
phases.description: The specific biases — anchoring, loss aversion, social proof, scarcity — that predictably distort how people judge value and take action.

phases.title: Behavior Change Models
phases.description: Frameworks for designing behavior itself: what has to be true for an action to happen, and how habits form and stick.

phases.title: Motivation & Engagement
phases.description: What actually drives people to keep engaging — the difference between internal and external motivators, and how gamification and flow keep people coming back.

phases.title: Applying Behavioral Psychology to Product & Marketing
phases.description: Turning the theory into practice — nudges, choice architecture, and where persuasive design crosses the line into manipulation.

phases.title: Behavioral Economics Fundamentals
phases.description: The economic side of the same ideas — how people actually value gains, losses, and money — plus a full free course to go deeper.

topics.title: System 1 vs. System 2 Thinking
topics.description: How the brain's fast, automatic thinking and its slow, deliberate thinking trade off in everyday decisions.

steps.d: For three decisions you make today, pause and note which felt automatic (System 1) versus deliberate (System 2).
Create a rule that requires people to slow down and think deliberately instead of relying on gut feel before a big decision.
In a meeting, identify a moment where someone is deciding quickly without full data and note what System 2 would do.
Take a decision you normally make fast, spend ten minutes thinking it through carefully, and compare the outcome.
Make a quick judgment on a real decision, analyze it deliberately, and write how your conclusion changed after deeper thinking.

topics.title: Heuristics: Mental Shortcuts in Decision-Making
topics.description: The rules of thumb people use to decide quickly, and why they help more often than they hurt.

steps.d: Name five rules of thumb you rely on without thinking, such as 'crowds know something important' or 'if I've heard of it, it's probably big'.
Take one of your heuristics, gather real data on a decision where it applies, and score how often it leads you right.
Identify a specific case where your favorite shortcut led you astray and explain what made that situation misleading.
Create a business process that deliberately uses a helpful heuristic while controlling for its weaknesses.
Explain one mental shortcut to a colleague with an example where it saved time and one where it could backfire.

topics.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow — Kahneman's Framework
topics.description: The book and researcher that turned System 1/2 thinking and dozens of biases into a shared vocabulary for the field.

steps.d: Pick a bias from the book (anchoring, availability, overconfidence) and give an example of how it shaped a real decision.
Read three decision-making stories and for each one name which Kahneman/Tversky bias is most likely at play.
Take one bias from the book and propose a specific process or rule that would nudge someone to decide more rationally.
Read one of Kahneman's classical studies, then find a place where your organization exhibits that same bias at scale.
Explain why people overweight losses and underweight unlikely gains, then give one example of how that changes a decision.

topics.title: Anchoring & Framing Effects
topics.description: How the first number you see and the way a choice is worded quietly shape the decision that follows.

steps.d: In a real or practice negotiation, go first and make an opening bid, and notice how it constrains the counterpart's response.
Take a business decision like budget cuts and reframe it positively like 'invest more strategically' to observe the emotional shift.
Ask ten people to estimate a number after giving either a high or low starting anchor and quantify the anchor's pull.
Review a deck, email, or pitch and identify where the framing is biasing the decision you're supposed to make.
Take an unpopular recommendation and reframe it (different words, different comparison) to make it more palatable.

topics.title: Loss Aversion & the Endowment Effect
topics.description: Why losing something feels worse than gaining the equivalent, and why owning something makes us overvalue it.

steps.d: List choices where losing something feels worse than gaining an equal amount would feel good.
Hold an object for five minutes, price what you'd pay to replace it if lost, then price what you'd accept to sell it.
Read a failed negotiation or deal and identify whether loss aversion (defending current state) was the barrier.
Take a decision people reject for loss-aversion reasons and rewrite it to feel less like giving something up.
Create a change initiative that improves efficiency but acknowledges that people feel the old way's loss keenly.

topics.title: Social Proof & Scarcity
topics.description: Why we copy what others are doing and want more of what seems limited or about to disappear.

steps.d: Look at a website or app and list every social proof element you see (reviews, testimonials, counts).
Visit three e-commerce sites, note which use scarcity language ('only 2 left', 'flash sale'), and score how much it moves you.
Identify an example where a company uses social proof misleadingly (fake reviews, old testimonials) and explain why it fails.
Propose an A/B test measuring how much 'people bought' language versus 'expert approved' language shifts conversion.
Plan a product launch with limited quantity, limited time, or exclusive access that leverages scarcity without deception.

topics.title: The Fogg Behavior Model
topics.description: BJ Fogg's model of exactly what has to line up — motivation, ability, and a prompt — for a behavior to happen.

steps.d: Take a behavior you want to encourage (profile completion, signup) and score how much motivation, ability, and prompt are present.
Identify a behavior people want to do but find hard, then propose three ways to simplify it.
Design a specific notification, text, or trigger that will prompt a desired behavior when motivation and ability are high.
Diagnose whether people aren't doing a behavior due to low motivation, low ability, or missing prompt, then fix motivation.
Implement one change based on Fogg (add prompt, boost ability, or increase relevance) and measure whether it moves the needle.

topics.title: Habit Loops: Cue, Routine, Reward
topics.description: How a repeated cue-routine-reward cycle turns a deliberate action into an automatic habit.

steps.d: Pick one automatic habit (coffee, checking email) and identify the cue, routine, and reward for that loop.
Take a habit you want to break and identify what psychological reward it delivers (stress relief, connection, entertainment).
Keep the same cue and reward as an existing habit but design a new routine that's better (replace scrolling with walking).
For a habit you want to keep, make the cue more obvious, routine easier, and reward more immediate and satisfying.
Attach a new desired habit to an existing automatic one—such as stretching right after coffee—and stick with it for four weeks.

topics.title: The Hook Model: Building Habit-Forming Products
topics.description: Nir Eyal's trigger-action-variable reward-investment loop for designing products people return to on their own.

steps.d: Pick a product you use often and trace one user action through trigger, action, variable reward, and investment.
For that product, pinpoint what makes the reward unpredictable enough to create curiosity (social feedback, points, content).
Notice how the product gets users to invest time, data, or effort to set up for the next loop.
Identify a product where the Hook Model isn't working (rewards too predictable, investments too costly) and propose a fix.
For a new feature, map its trigger, action, variable reward, and investment to form a habit.

topics.title: Intrinsic vs. Extrinsic Motivation
topics.description: The difference between doing something because it's rewarding in itself and doing it for an outside reward or to avoid a penalty.

steps.d: Name five things you do without external reward and identify what the internal reward actually is.
Find a real example where adding a reward (money, points, competition) made people care less, not more.
Read three task scenarios and for each say whether extrinsic rewards are likely to help or hurt performance.
Take a task people find boring and redesign it to feel more autonomous, meaningful, or competent.
Ask your team what moves them most (autonomy, impact, mastery, money, security) and act on the pattern.

topics.title: Gamification & the Octalysis Framework
topics.description: Yu-kai Chou's map of the eight core human drives that game-like design elements tap into.

steps.d: Take a gamified product and identify which of Yu-kai Chou's eight drives (epic meaning, accomplishment, empowerment, ownership, social influence, scarcity, unpredictability, loss) it's tapping.
Notice which of the eight drives is underutilized in that product and propose one feature that would activate it.
Propose a metric or leaderboard that taps one drive without being exploitative (recognize collaboration, not just individual wins).
Look at a heavily gamified product and identify which mechanics are addictive versus manipulative or harmful.
Take a process people dread (expense reports, training) and propose how you'd use one or two drives to make it engaging.

topics.title: Flow, Feedback Loops & Engagement Design
topics.description: Csikszentmihalyi's flow state, and why fast, clear feedback is what keeps people absorbed in a task or product.

steps.d: Track yourself for one day and identify moments when you lost track of time and felt fully engaged.
Take a task you started in flow but quit and identify whether challenge became too hard (anxiety) or too easy (boredom).
For a tedious work process (data entry, testing), propose a feedback mechanism that shows progress in real time.
For a learning task or game, propose how you'd adjust difficulty dynamically as people's skill increases to stay in flow.
Design a dashboard showing users exactly how they're progressing on a goal, with milestones and clear next steps.

topics.title: Interface Fundamentals Behind Behavioural Design
topics.description: The usability basics the next two topics assume: heuristics, cognitive load and visual hierarchy.

steps.t: Audit one screen against the ten heuristics
steps.d: Take an app you use daily and mark where it satisfies and where it breaks each of Nielsen's ten usability heuristics.

steps.t: Count the decisions on one page
steps.d: List every choice a page asks of you. That count is its cognitive load, and it is almost always higher than the designer intended.
On one screen, note what your eye reaches first, second and third, then work out which of size, contrast, position or whitespace did it.

steps.t: Draw the same control two ways
steps.d: Sketch one action button that makes the action obvious and one that buries it, and name the technique each uses.
Take a form that annoyed you, redraw it with fewer fields and a clearer order, and say which heuristic the original broke.

topics.title: Nudge Theory & Choice Architecture
topics.description: How the way options are presented — the default, the order, the framing — steers decisions without removing any choice.

steps.d: Look at a website, form, or public process and spot three ways the design nudges choices (defaults, order, framing).
Propose changing what's pre-selected as default—opt-out versus opt-in for a feature—and predict how it shifts user behavior.
Take a menu or selection screen and reorder options so the socially beneficial or easiest choice appears first or defaults.
For an overwhelming decision (insurance plans, phone contracts), propose how you'd re-architect choices to reduce burden.
If designing a benefits enrollment or savings decision from zero, what order, defaults, and framing would nudge the right choice.

topics.title: Dark Patterns & the Ethics of Persuasion
topics.description: Where nudging crosses into deception, and the manipulative UX patterns regulators are now cracking down on.

steps.d: Find a dark pattern on a real website (roach motel, misdirection, hidden costs) and explain what it manipulates.
Debate whether a design choice is a nudge (ethical) or dark pattern (manipulation) and label it and explain.
For a dark pattern, estimate customer cost: lost trust, churn, regulatory risk, or brand damage.
Take a real dark pattern and propose achieving the same business goal without the manipulation.
Review a product you work on, find one design choice that might feel manipulative, and fix it.

topics.title: Behavioral Design in Marketing & UX
topics.description: Applying behavioral science deliberately inside product and marketing design, rather than bolting psychology on after the fact.

steps.d: Find a real ad or landing page and identify what psychological principle it's using (social proof, scarcity, loss, FOMO).
Take a checkout, sign-up, or onboarding sequence and propose two changes based on behavioral principles.
Propose an A/B test measuring whether 'people bought' language versus 'expert approved' language shifts conversion.
Design a metric tracking whether a behavioral change moved the outcome you cared about (signup, purchase, retention).
Prioritize three UX improvements based on behavioral science rather than feature requests or vanity metrics.

topics.title: Prospect Theory
topics.description: Kahneman and Tversky's model of how people actually weigh risky gains and losses, and why it beats the classical rational-agent model.

steps.d: Take a high-stakes decision and map what the reference point is, what feels like gain, and what feels like loss.
Find a business situation where decisions are anchored on the wrong reference point, leading to suboptimal choices.
Create a pricing, policy, or offer that accounts for losses looming twice as large as equivalent gains.
For a risk-averse decision, propose reframing that shows the bigger risk is actually staying in status quo.
Based on how your team experiences gains and losses, propose one strategic shift that feels less scary or more compelling.

topics.title: Mental Accounting
topics.description: Why people mentally sort money into separate 'accounts' and treat a dollar differently depending on where it came from.

steps.d: Track spending for one week and notice which mental bucket each purchase goes into and whether logic is rational.
Propose a pricing or bundling change that moves an expensive item into a different mental account to feel cheaper.
Find a business where mental accounting creates illogical decisions such as cutting marketing budget while leaving project contingencies untouched.
For a customer treating spending domains separately, propose a way to help them see the holistic picture.
Create a savings tool or budget system that uses mental accounting to help people save more.

topics.title: Intro to Behavioral Economics
topics.description: A field-level overview of behavioral economics, plus a full free course for going deeper than any single article can.

steps.d: Skim an article connecting all behavioral economics and write one sentence on why it matters versus classical economics.
Find one real pricing, investment, or consumption behavior that classical economics can't explain but behavioral economics can.
Explain to an economics-trained colleague why people don't always maximize utility with one surprising example.
Enroll in the University of Toronto's free Behavioral Economics course on edX and complete at least three weeks.
Pick a field you work in and propose one decision change based on behavioral economics insight.
